rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid missing late compounds. This should show whether peaks are compressed early, eluting in the hold, or spread across the gradient, guiding later narrowing and slope optimization.

All 10 peaks eluted well within the gradient, so trim the gradient window to the observed elution range to spend the run where the peaks are and reduce the time penalty. Keeping tG and T fixed isolates the effect of the narrower phi window on the moderately close mid-cluster around peaks 5–7.

The broad window was clearly better, so now test slope directly by halving tG while keeping phi and temperature fixed. This will show whether the critical mid-cluster is slope-sensitive and may improve CRF by shortening the run without sacrificing too much resolution.

The close 5–7 cluster is strongly slope-sensitive: compressing to 10 min collapsed it, while 20 min separated it well. An intermediate tG should keep run time short while restoring enough resolution to improve on the current best CRF.

The optimum appears between 14 and 20 min, with the 6/7 pair improving steadily as tG increases. Testing 16 min should retain zero time penalty while potentially pushing the worst-pair resolution high enough to reach the CRF maximum.

The 6/7 pair remains the only critical pair and is slope-sensitive, but 14 min is already near the best time tradeoff. A modest temperature change is the cleanest next lever to test whether selectivity around that pair improves without adding a time penalty.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity dramatically, so test the opposite direction at the current near-optimal 14 min slope. If the critical cluster reorders or spreads at higher temperature, this could beat the current best without increasing run time.

Temperature moves both hurt the critical cluster, so return to 40 C and continue optimizing slope. Since 16 min fully resolved the close pairs but incurred only a small time penalty, 18 min tests whether extra resolution gain can offset that penalty better than either 16 or 20 min.

The optimum is dominated by the 14 min, 40 C method, so now probe whether a slightly lower phi1 can improve selectivity in the late-mid cluster without pushing the run into a time penalty. All peaks were out by 9.4 min, so there is room to trim the high-organic end modestly while keeping every compound in-gradient.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the near-critical 6/7 pair while keeping zero time penalty, so continue in the same direction. A further small reduction to 0.85 may give the last bit of selectivity needed to maximize CRF while still keeping all compounds within the gradient.

At phi1 0.90 the method is very close to ideal with zero time penalty, so now test whether a slightly steeper gradient can shorten the late tail while preserving enough selectivity in the 6/7 pair. This directly probes whether the current optimum is broad or if there is a better time/selectivity balance nearby.

With phi1 0.90, shortening to 12 min hurt the critical 6/7 pair, so the optimum likely lies slightly shallower than 14 min rather than steeper. Testing 16 min checks whether the gain in selectivity at this better phi window can outweigh a small time penalty and surpass the current best.

The best method is very close to ideal, so use remaining space to probe whether a larger temperature shift can improve the stubborn 6/7 selectivity at the winning phi window. Since 35 C and 45 C were both worse at phi1 0.95, this is a low-probability but still plausible way to gain the last increment toward CRF 1.0.

Temperature excursions are clearly harmful, so return to 40 C and fine-tune the low end of the gradient window. Raising phi0 slightly may move the crowded mid-cluster to a more favorable part of the gradient and improve the remaining 6/7 separation without much impact on runtime.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF again, so continue that trend while keeping the successful upper bound and slope fixed. This should test whether the critical 6/7 pair benefits from a further upward shift of the gradient window toward the actual elution region.

The best result so far came from phi0 0.10 and phi1 0.90, while lowering either boundary alone changed selectivity in useful ways. Combining the improved lower bound with the lower upper bound may give a slightly better placement of the whole peak cluster and push the critical pair to the maximum CRF.

We have already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000, so there is no way to improve on the objective. This run explores the nearby plateau around the optimum and checks robustness of the successful narrowed window in case multiple methods also score perfectly.

With multiple perfect methods already found, map the robustness plateau by shifting the lower bound upward one more step while keeping the successful upper bound and slope fixed. This checks how far the optimum extends before the earliest peaks become too compressed or effectively unretained.

The perfect region includes phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85, so now test whether the upper bound can be trimmed one more step while preserving full in-gradient elution. This maps the lower edge of the robust optimum and may yield another perfect method with a slightly tighter gradient window.

Since lowering phi1 to 0.80 increased runtime at phi0 0.10, test whether shifting the whole window upward restores the favorable placement seen for the perfect methods. This completes a useful check of the neighboring plateau while staying near the proven optimum region.

With the objective already maxed out, use remaining runs to stress-test the best window. This checks whether a combined temperature decrease and steeper slope causes the known critical cluster to collapse, helping define the boundaries of robustness around the optimal method.

The best region is clearly around phi0 0.10–0.15, phi1 0.85, tG 14 at 40 C, so with the score already maxed out, test a slightly shallower version of the second perfect method. This helps define whether the perfect plateau extends to longer gradients at the same narrowed window.

With only a few runs left and the score already at the maximum, use this to probe temperature robustness of the best-performing window itself. This tells whether the perfect method is narrowly centered at 40 C or whether the narrowed phi window also tolerates a hotter condition.

The perfect methods are both at 14 min and 40 C, so use one of the final injections to test the steeper boundary of that perfect plateau for the shifted window. This checks whether phi0 0.15, phi1 0.85 remains perfect at shorter tG or if the critical cluster collapses as seen in other steeper runs.

Use the final injection to complete the temperature robustness map of the best overall window at the coldest allowed setting. We already know 40 C is optimal and hotter is worse; this last run defines the low-temperature boundary around the proven perfect method.
